1.question: What is Path loss?
options: A sudden hardware fault that mutes only the base-station clock.
A coding overhead added so the receiver can detect bit errors.
The time an idle phone waits before it answers a page.
Reduction in received radio power as the transmitter and receiver move farther apart.
1.correctAnswer: Reduction in received radio power as the transmitter and receiver move farther apart.
1.explanation: Radiated energy spreads and is absorbed, so less power arrives as range increases.

1.question: What is Free-space path loss?
options: Loss that appears only when two cells reuse one channel.
Line-of-sight power loss caused only by geometric spreading, with no obstacles or ground reflections.
Loss caused by hills blocking an otherwise short radio hop.
Loss inserted by a channel code before modulation.
1.correctAnswer: Line-of-sight power loss caused only by geometric spreading, with no obstacles or ground reflections.
1.explanation: In free space the same energy is spread over a larger sphere as range grows.

1.question: What is Multipath propagation?
options: Encryption of one packet into several cipher blocks.
A single optical fibre path from a studio to a tower.
Travel of one transmitted signal along several reflected, diffracted, or scattered paths.
Transmission of independent users on separate assigned frequencies.
1.correctAnswer: Travel of one transmitted signal along several reflected, diffracted, or scattered paths.
1.explanation: Buildings and the ground create copies that arrive at different times.

1.question: What is Fading?
options: A fixed amplifier gain chosen once when the site is built.
A scheduled reduction of transmit power at night.
The steady loss of a cable of unchanging length.
Variation of received signal strength over time or position caused by multipath or obstruction.
1.correctAnswer: Variation of received signal strength over time or position caused by multipath or obstruction.
1.explanation: Multipath copies add and cancel, and obstacles change, so amplitude is not steady.

1.question: What is Rayleigh fading?
options: Slow blockage by a single large building only.
Fading dominated by one strong direct path plus weak echoes.
A purely deterministic loss that never varies with position.
Small-scale fading when many scattered paths arrive and no line-of-sight path dominates.
1.correctAnswer: Small-scale fading when many scattered paths arrive and no line-of-sight path dominates.
1.explanation: With no dominant path the quadrature components are roughly Gaussian, so the envelope is Rayleigh.

1.question: What is Rician fading?
options: Fading with no dominant path at all.
Interference from a neighbouring frequency plan.
Only the slow shadow of a hill, with no multipath.
Small-scale fading when a strong line-of-sight path arrives together with weaker scattered paths.
1.correctAnswer: Small-scale fading when a strong line-of-sight path arrives together with weaker scattered paths.
1.explanation: The steady direct component changes the envelope from Rayleigh to Rician.

1.question: What is Shadowing?
options: Fast ripple of amplitude over a few wavelengths from multipath.
Intentional power reduction commanded by the scheduler.
Slow change in local-mean received power caused by large obstacles blocking the path.
A Doppler shift of the carrier frequency.
1.correctAnswer: Slow change in local-mean received power caused by large obstacles blocking the path.
1.explanation: Hills and buildings attenuate the whole signal for many metres, unlike fast multipath ripple.

1.question: What is Doppler shift?
options: A phase code applied by the modulator on purpose.
A frequency error from an unlicensed Wi-Fi channel plan.
Change in observed carrier frequency when transmitter and receiver move relative to each other.
A time offset caused only by a longer propagation path.
1.correctAnswer: Change in observed carrier frequency when transmitter and receiver move relative to each other.
1.explanation: Motion changes how fast wave crests arrive, so the received frequency moves.

1.question: What is Coherence time?
options: The time interval over which the channel impulse response stays approximately constant.
The gap between the first and last multipath echoes.
The frequency band over which fading stays correlated.
The slot length assigned to one GSM user.
1.correctAnswer: The time interval over which the channel impulse response stays approximately constant.
1.explanation: Motion changes multipath phases at a rate set by Doppler spread, which fixes this interval.

1.question: What is Coherence bandwidth?
options: The Doppler shift of the fastest user.
The range of frequencies over which the channel gain remains highly correlated.
The total licensed spectrum of an operator.
The time for which a channel estimate stays valid.
1.correctAnswer: The range of frequencies over which the channel gain remains highly correlated.
1.explanation: Large delay spread makes frequencies fade differently, so this range becomes narrower.

2.question: What is Delay spread?
options: The time span between the earliest and latest significant copies of a multipath signal.
How long the channel gain stays constant in time.
The duration of one OFDM cyclic prefix by definition only.
The round-trip time of a core-network ping.
2.correctAnswer: The time span between the earliest and latest significant copies of a multipath signal.
2.explanation: Different path lengths make copies of the same symbol arrive spread out in time.

2.question: What is Flat fading?
options: A fade that always changes inside one symbol.
Fading that puts a deep notch in only part of the signal band.
Interference that arrives only from the adjacent carrier.
Fading in which every frequency in the signal bandwidth sees nearly the same gain.
2.correctAnswer: Fading in which every frequency in the signal bandwidth sees nearly the same gain.
2.explanation: This occurs when the signal bandwidth is much smaller than the coherence bandwidth.

2.question: What is Frequency-selective fading?
options: Slow shadowing that is identical at every frequency.
Fading that scales the whole signal spectrum by one gain.
A filter that removes an entire licensed band on purpose.
Fading in which different frequencies inside the signal bandwidth experience different gains.
2.correctAnswer: Fading in which different frequencies inside the signal bandwidth experience different gains.
2.explanation: A large delay spread makes the frequency response vary and can cause inter-symbol interference.

2.question: What is Fast fading?
options: Fading that changes appreciably within one symbol, so the gain is not constant over that symbol.
Fading that stays fixed for many symbols.
A shadow that changes only when the user turns a corner.
Fading that is identical on every subcarrier.
2.correctAnswer: Fading that changes appreciably within one symbol, so the gain is not constant over that symbol.
2.explanation: The coherence time is then shorter than the symbol duration.

2.question: What is Slow fading?
options: Fading that stays nearly constant over many successive symbols.
Fading that changes inside every symbol.
An instantaneous Doppler jump once per bit.
A different gain on every subcarrier at one instant.
2.correctAnswer: Fading that stays nearly constant over many successive symbols.
2.explanation: The coherence time is then much longer than the symbol duration, so one estimate covers a burst.

2.question: What is Cell?
options: A location area made of many sites used only for paging.
The core-network database that stores subscriber profiles.
The geographic service area covered by one base-station site and its radio channels.
The entire country served by one mobile operator.
2.correctAnswer: The geographic service area covered by one base-station site and its radio channels.
2.explanation: Users in that area are served by that site, which is the basic unit of a cellular plan.

2.question: What is Frequency reuse?
options: Hopping a single call across all channels each burst.
Encrypting the same bits with a repeated cipher key.
Giving every cell in the network a completely unique band.
Assigning the same carrier frequencies again in cells that are far enough apart.
2.correctAnswer: Assigning the same carrier frequencies again in cells that are far enough apart.
2.explanation: Distance lowers co-channel interference, so a limited band can serve many cells.

2.question: What is Cluster size?
options: The number of sectors on a single tower.
The radius of a cell measured in kilometres.
The number of time slots inside one GSM frame.
The number of cells that together use each channel once before the reuse pattern repeats.
2.correctAnswer: The number of cells that together use each channel once before the reuse pattern repeats.
2.explanation: A larger cluster separates co-channel cells more, trading capacity per cell for less interference.

2.question: What is Co-channel interference?
options: Leakage from a transmitter on the next carrier frequency.
Interference from other transmitters that operate on the same carrier frequency.
Noise generated inside the receiver's own electronics.
A delayed copy of the wanted signal from the same transmitter.
2.correctAnswer: Interference from other transmitters that operate on the same carrier frequency.
2.explanation: Reuse places the same channel in other cells, and those signals enter the victim receiver.

2.question: What is Adjacent-channel interference?
options: Noise that does not depend on any other transmitter.
Interference from a distant cell on the identical carrier.
Interference from energy that leaks into the receiver from a neighbouring carrier.
A fade caused only by two multipath copies cancelling.
2.correctAnswer: Interference from energy that leaks into the receiver from a neighbouring carrier.
2.explanation: Imperfect filters and transmitter masks let nearby frequencies spill into the wanted channel.

3.question: What is Handover?
options: An idle phone's report that it entered a new location area.
The first registration after the phone is switched on.
Transfer of an ongoing mobile connection from one base station to another.
A broadcast asking an idle phone to answer a call.
3.correctAnswer: Transfer of an ongoing mobile connection from one base station to another.
3.explanation: As the user moves, the radio link must follow the cell with the better signal.

3.question: What is Hard handover?
options: A cell change that releases the old radio link before the new link is established.
A cell change that keeps two base-station links up together.
A core-network restart that drops every session.
An idle reselections with no active call.
3.correctAnswer: A cell change that releases the old radio link before the new link is established.
3.explanation: The mobile cannot hold both channels at once, so there is a short break-before-make gap.

3.question: What is Soft handover?
options: A forced release of the call when load is high.
A break-before-make change that uses only one link at a time.
A cell change during which the mobile keeps radio links to more than one base station.
A change of IP address with no radio involvement.
3.correctAnswer: A cell change during which the mobile keeps radio links to more than one base station.
3.explanation: CDMA can combine the same signal from several sites before one link is dropped.

3.question: What is Handover hysteresis?
options: The delay added by a speech transcoder.
The minimum power a phone may use on any channel.
An extra signal margin a neighbour must exceed before a handover is allowed.
The number of cells in a reuse cluster.
3.correctAnswer: An extra signal margin a neighbour must exceed before a handover is allowed.
3.explanation: The margin stops switching when two cell signals are nearly equal and fluctuating.

3.question: What is Ping-pong handover?
options: An idle phone updating its location once per day.
Rapid repeated handovers of the same connection back and forth between two cells.
A single successful move from a weak cell to a strong cell.
Combining two downlinks without releasing either.
3.correctAnswer: Rapid repeated handovers of the same connection back and forth between two cells.
3.explanation: Signal fluctuation around a tight threshold reverses the handover decision again and again.

3.question: What is Location update?
options: A move of an active traffic channel to a new cell.
A network broadcast searching for one idle phone.
A message from an idle mobile reporting that it has entered a new location area.
A measurement of neighbour cells during a call.
3.correctAnswer: A message from an idle mobile reporting that it has entered a new location area.
3.explanation: The network stores that area so it later knows where to page the mobile.

3.question: What is Paging?
options: Transfer of an active call to a stronger cell.
A network broadcast that asks one specific idle mobile to respond to an incoming session.
A request for an uplink grant to send a photo.
An idle mobile telling the network its new location area.
3.correctAnswer: A network broadcast that asks one specific idle mobile to respond to an incoming session.
3.explanation: The network often knows only the location area, so it calls the mobile across that area.

3.question: What is GSM?
options: A fourth-generation system with OFDMA and an all-IP core.
A second-generation cellular standard that uses TDMA and GMSK on 200 kHz carriers.
An analogue first-generation system with one FM channel per user.
A short-range personal radio that hops in the 2.4 GHz band.
3.correctAnswer: A second-generation cellular standard that uses TDMA and GMSK on 200 kHz carriers.
3.explanation: GSM carries digital voice in eight time slots on each 200 kHz GMSK carrier.

3.question: What is TDMA?
options: Letting every user transmit whenever the channel looks idle.
Sharing one carrier by giving each user a distinct repeating time slot.
Separating users only by spreading codes.
Giving each user a separate frequency at the same time.
3.correctAnswer: Sharing one carrier by giving each user a distinct repeating time slot.
3.explanation: Users transmit in turn, so they are separated in time on the same frequency.

3.question: What is FDMA?
options: Assigning users different time slots on one shared carrier.
Assigning groups of orthogonal subcarriers that can change each slot.
Sharing a band by assigning each user a distinct frequency channel.
Assigning users different spreading codes on one carrier.
3.correctAnswer: Sharing a band by assigning each user a distinct frequency channel.
3.explanation: Filters and guard bands keep users apart because they occupy different frequencies together.

4.question: What is CDMA?
options: Serving only one user in the whole cell at a time.
Sharing time and frequency while separating users with unique spreading codes.
Separating users only by time slot.
Separating users only by carrier frequency.
4.correctAnswer: Sharing time and frequency while separating users with unique spreading codes.
4.explanation: A receiver despreads its own code and treats other users as interference.

4.question: What is OFDMA?
options: Giving each user one wide non-overlapping analogue channel.
Letting stations contend with random backoff.
Sharing a band by assigning different groups of orthogonal subcarriers to different users.
Separating users only with spreading codes.
4.correctAnswer: Sharing a band by assigning different groups of orthogonal subcarriers to different users.
4.explanation: Orthogonal subcarriers can be packed tightly and grouped to follow each user's channel.

4.question: What is LTE?
options: A 3G wideband CDMA system with a circuit-switched core.
A 2G system of eight GMSK time slots on 200 kHz.
A fourth-generation cellular system using OFDMA downlink, SC-FDMA uplink, and an all-IP core.
A personal-area hop radio for headsets.
4.correctAnswer: A fourth-generation cellular system using OFDMA downlink, SC-FDMA uplink, and an all-IP core.
4.explanation: LTE schedules packet data on a shared OFDMA carrier and does not use circuit-switched radio bearers.

4.question: What is 5G NR?
options: The fifth-generation New Radio interface, with scalable subcarrier spacing and massive MIMO support.
A 2G standard locked to 200 kHz GMSK carriers.
A wireless LAN standard in the IEEE 802.11 family.
A 4G system whose subcarrier spacing is fixed at 15 kHz.
4.correctAnswer: The fifth-generation New Radio interface, with scalable subcarrier spacing and massive MIMO support.
4.explanation: NR numerology lets one design serve wide millimetre-wave carriers and short low-latency slots.

4.question: What is Small cell?
options: A handset operating as a measuring tool only.
A core router that switches packets between cities.
A low-power base station that covers a short range, such as a street, room, or venue.
A high tower planned to cover several kilometres.
4.correctAnswer: A low-power base station that covers a short range, such as a street, room, or venue.
4.explanation: Short range lets spectrum be reused densely and fills gaps a macro site covers poorly.

4.question: What is MIMO?
options: Repeating one stream on separated antennas only to survive a fade.
Hopping one stream across many carriers.
Use of multiple antennas at both ends to send several spatial data streams on one frequency.
Assigning each antenna a different licensed band.
4.correctAnswer: Use of multiple antennas at both ends to send several spatial data streams on one frequency.
4.explanation: Scattering makes the spatial paths different enough for the receiver to separate the streams.

4.question: What is Beamforming?
options: Compressing the user data before transmission.
Weighting an antenna array so more radiated energy is aimed toward a chosen user.
Splitting users by orthogonal codes.
Radiating equally in every direction from one dipole.
4.correctAnswer: Weighting an antenna array so more radiated energy is aimed toward a chosen user.
4.explanation: Phase weights make the waves add toward the user and partly cancel elsewhere.

4.question: What is Massive MIMO?
options: A base-station array with very many antennas serving many users on the same time-frequency resources.
Two antennas used only to pick the stronger branch.
A Wi-Fi contention network with one antenna.
A single rooftop dipole covering a sector.
4.correctAnswer: A base-station array with very many antennas serving many users on the same time-frequency resources.
4.explanation: Dozens or hundreds of antennas form tight beams and separate users in space.

4.question: What is Wi-Fi?
options: The IEEE 802.11 family of wireless local-area networks, usually operated in unlicensed bands.
A licensed cellular standard with a SIM and a core network.
A wired Ethernet standard over twisted pair.
A one-hop satellite broadcast toward fixed dishes.
4.correctAnswer: The IEEE 802.11 family of wireless local-area networks, usually operated in unlicensed bands.
4.explanation: 802.11 defines wireless LAN frames, contention access, and bands such as 2.4 and 5 GHz.

4.question: What is CSMA/CA?
options: A Wi-Fi access method that listens for a busy medium and waits a random backoff before sending.
Sending immediately with no sensing and no backoff.
Detecting collisions on a coaxial cable while transmitting.
A base station assigning every user a fixed slot.
4.correctAnswer: A Wi-Fi access method that listens for a busy medium and waits a random backoff before sending.
4.explanation: A wireless sender cannot reliably hear a collision while it transmits, so it tries to avoid one.

5.question: What is Hidden node?
options: A node whose signal captures the receiver despite a weaker collision.
A station that defers because it hears a sender, though its own destination is clear.
A station that cannot hear another sender even though both can collide at the same receiver.
Two phones separated by codes on a CDMA carrier.
5.correctAnswer: A station that cannot hear another sender even though both can collide at the same receiver.
5.explanation: Distance or an obstacle hides one sender, so carrier sense does not prevent a collision.

5.question: What is Bluetooth?
options: A wireless LAN access-point standard for whole buildings.
A short-range personal-area radio that frequency-hops in the 2.4 GHz band.
A long-haul microwave link between hilltop towers.
A cellular wide-area standard managed by a mobile operator.
5.correctAnswer: A short-range personal-area radio that frequency-hops in the 2.4 GHz band.
5.explanation: Classic Bluetooth hops among 79 one-megahertz channels to live with other 2.4 GHz users.

5.question: What is Frequency hopping?
options: Spreading each bit by a fast code while staying on one carrier.
Keeping one fixed channel for the whole session.
Assigning a permanent frequency in a cellular cluster plan.
Changing the carrier many times per second using a sequence known to both ends.
5.correctAnswer: Changing the carrier many times per second using a sequence known to both ends.
5.explanation: A narrow interferer then damages only some hops, and the link can recover the others.

5.question: What is QPSK?
options: A modulation with only two phases, carrying one bit per symbol.
On-off keying that turns the carrier on or off.
A square grid that uses several amplitudes as well as phases.
A modulation that maps each two-bit group to one of four carrier phases 90 degrees apart.
5.correctAnswer: A modulation that maps each two-bit group to one of four carrier phases 90 degrees apart.
5.explanation: Four phases carry two bits per symbol and can keep a constant envelope.

5.question: What is QAM?
options: A modulation that encodes bits in both the amplitude and the phase of the carrier.
A two-phase modulation that carries only one bit per symbol.
Frequency-shift keying between two tones.
Pulse-position modulation with a constant carrier amplitude.
5.correctAnswer: A modulation that encodes bits in both the amplitude and the phase of the carrier.
5.explanation: A rectangular constellation packs several bits into one symbol when the link is strong enough.

5.question: What is Link adaptation?
options: Changing modulation and coding during a session to match the current channel quality.
Planning reuse distances on a paper frequency map.
Keeping one constellation and code rate for the whole session.
Authenticating the SIM before any data flows.
5.correctAnswer: Changing modulation and coding during a session to match the current channel quality.
5.explanation: A strong channel can use a denser constellation, while a weak channel needs a tougher mode.

5.question: What is Spatial diversity?
options: Carrying the same information on separated antennas so one fade is unlikely to hit every copy.
Compressing the source to fewer bits.
Splitting a site into directional sectors with different channels.
Sending independent data streams on the same antennas.
5.correctAnswer: Carrying the same information on separated antennas so one fade is unlikely to hit every copy.
5.explanation: Antennas spaced by a fraction of a wavelength see partly independent multipath.

5.question: What is Sectorisation?
options: Hopping every sector through the same single channel.
Combining two sites during a soft handover.
Covering the whole site with one omnidirectional antenna.
Dividing one site into angular sectors, each served by a directional antenna.
5.correctAnswer: Dividing one site into angular sectors, each served by a directional antenna.
5.explanation: Each sector sees a smaller angle of interference and can carry its own channels.

5.question: What is Mobility management?
options: Manufacturing the handset antenna.
Compressing speech before it enters the channel coder.
Billing the subscriber at the end of the month.
Network functions that track where a mobile is and keep its session as it moves between cells.
5.correctAnswer: Network functions that track where a mobile is and keep its session as it moves between cells.
5.explanation: It includes idle-area tracking and active handover so reachability and sessions survive motion.

5.question: What is SINR?
options: Received signal strength with no comparison to interference or noise.
The delay between the first and last multipath echoes.
The number of cells that share one reuse pattern.
The ratio of wanted signal power to the sum of interference power and noise power.
5.correctAnswer: The ratio of wanted signal power to the sum of interference power and noise power.
5.explanation: Both interference and noise corrupt symbols, so schedulers and decoders use this ratio.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Path loss?
options: Walking a few metres indoors makes phone signal bars rise and fall although the tower is unchanged.
A clear satellite downlink loses power with both distance and carrier frequency.
A handset two kilometres from a tower receives far less power than one at 200 metres.
On a city street the same beacon reaches a phone from a wall, a bus, and the road.
6.correctAnswer: A handset two kilometres from a tower receives far less power than one at 200 metres.
6.explanation: Radiated energy spreads and is absorbed, so less power arrives as range increases.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Free-space path loss?
options: On a city street the same beacon reaches a phone from a wall, a bus, and the road.
A downtown pedestrian whose tower is hidden by blocks of flats sees a Rayleigh envelope.
Walking a few metres indoors makes phone signal bars rise and fall although the tower is unchanged.
A clear satellite downlink loses power with both distance and carrier frequency.
6.correctAnswer: A clear satellite downlink loses power with both distance and carrier frequency.
6.explanation: In free space the same energy is spread over a larger sphere as range grows.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Multipath propagation?
options: A downtown pedestrian whose tower is hidden by blocks of flats sees a Rayleigh envelope.
A drone that can see a rooftop radio, while still catching wall echoes, experiences Rician fading.
On a city street the same beacon reaches a phone from a wall, a bus, and the road.
Walking a few metres indoors makes phone signal bars rise and fall although the tower is unchanged.
6.correctAnswer: On a city street the same beacon reaches a phone from a wall, a bus, and the road.
6.explanation: Buildings and the ground create copies that arrive at different times.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Fading?
options: A downtown pedestrian whose tower is hidden by blocks of flats sees a Rayleigh envelope.
Driving behind a hill drops a call's average level by about 10 dB until the ridge clears.
Walking a few metres indoors makes phone signal bars rise and fall although the tower is unchanged.
A drone that can see a rooftop radio, while still catching wall echoes, experiences Rician fading.
6.correctAnswer: Walking a few metres indoors makes phone signal bars rise and fall although the tower is unchanged.
6.explanation: Multipath copies add and cancel, and obstacles change, so amplitude is not steady.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Rayleigh fading?
options: Driving behind a hill drops a call's average level by about 10 dB until the ridge clears.
A downtown pedestrian whose tower is hidden by blocks of flats sees a Rayleigh envelope.
A drone that can see a rooftop radio, while still catching wall echoes, experiences Rician fading.
A handset in a car approaching a tower hears a slightly higher carrier than the one transmitted.
6.correctAnswer: A downtown pedestrian whose tower is hidden by blocks of flats sees a Rayleigh envelope.
6.explanation: With no dominant path the quadrature components are roughly Gaussian, so the envelope is Rayleigh.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Rician fading?
options: A pedestrian channel stays similar for milliseconds, while a bullet-train channel changes sooner.
Driving behind a hill drops a call's average level by about 10 dB until the ridge clears.
A drone that can see a rooftop radio, while still catching wall echoes, experiences Rician fading.
A handset in a car approaching a tower hears a slightly higher carrier than the one transmitted.
6.correctAnswer: A drone that can see a rooftop radio, while still catching wall echoes, experiences Rician fading.
6.explanation: The steady direct component changes the envelope from Rayleigh to Rician.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Shadowing?
options: A channel with tiny delay spread stays correlated across a whole 200 kHz GSM carrier.
A handset in a car approaching a tower hears a slightly higher carrier than the one transmitted.
Driving behind a hill drops a call's average level by about 10 dB until the ridge clears.
A pedestrian channel stays similar for milliseconds, while a bullet-train channel changes sooner.
6.correctAnswer: Driving behind a hill drops a call's average level by about 10 dB until the ridge clears.
6.explanation: Hills and buildings attenuate the whole signal for many metres, unlike fast multipath ripple.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Doppler shift?
options: A pedestrian channel stays similar for milliseconds, while a bullet-train channel changes sooner.
In a hilly suburb the last strong echo of a pulse arrives 3 microseconds after the first.
A handset in a car approaching a tower hears a slightly higher carrier than the one transmitted.
A channel with tiny delay spread stays correlated across a whole 200 kHz GSM carrier.
6.correctAnswer: A handset in a car approaching a tower hears a slightly higher carrier than the one transmitted.
6.explanation: Motion changes how fast wave crests arrive, so the received frequency moves.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Coherence time?
options: A pedestrian channel stays similar for milliseconds, while a bullet-train channel changes sooner.
A narrowband paging tone fades up and down as a whole, with no notch inside its spectrum.
A channel with tiny delay spread stays correlated across a whole 200 kHz GSM carrier.
In a hilly suburb the last strong echo of a pulse arrives 3 microseconds after the first.
6.correctAnswer: A pedestrian channel stays similar for milliseconds, while a bullet-train channel changes sooner.
6.explanation: Motion changes multipath phases at a rate set by Doppler spread, which fixes this interval.

6.question: Which situation illustrates Coherence bandwidth?
options: An urban LTE resource block shows a deep notch on some subcarriers but not on others.
A narrowband paging tone fades up and down as a whole, with no notch inside its spectrum.
A channel with tiny delay spread stays correlated across a whole 200 kHz GSM carrier.
In a hilly suburb the last strong echo of a pulse arrives 3 microseconds after the first.
6.correctAnswer: A channel with tiny delay spread stays correlated across a whole 200 kHz GSM carrier.
6.explanation: Large delay spread makes frequencies fade differently, so this range becomes narrower.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Delay spread?
options: An urban LTE resource block shows a deep notch on some subcarriers but not on others.
A very long satellite symbol changes gain before it ends because the terminal is moving quickly.
A narrowband paging tone fades up and down as a whole, with no notch inside its spectrum.
In a hilly suburb the last strong echo of a pulse arrives 3 microseconds after the first.
7.correctAnswer: In a hilly suburb the last strong echo of a pulse arrives 3 microseconds after the first.
7.explanation: Different path lengths make copies of the same symbol arrive spread out in time.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Flat fading?
options: A very long satellite symbol changes gain before it ends because the terminal is moving quickly.
A narrowband paging tone fades up and down as a whole, with no notch inside its spectrum.
An urban LTE resource block shows a deep notch on some subcarriers but not on others.
At walking speed an LTE channel estimate is reused across a subframe because the fade is slow.
7.correctAnswer: A narrowband paging tone fades up and down as a whole, with no notch inside its spectrum.
7.explanation: This occurs when the signal bandwidth is much smaller than the coherence bandwidth.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Frequency-selective fading?
options: A suburban tower planned for about a 2 kilometre radius forms one cell on the operator map.
A very long satellite symbol changes gain before it ends because the terminal is moving quickly.
An urban LTE resource block shows a deep notch on some subcarriers but not on others.
At walking speed an LTE channel estimate is reused across a subframe because the fade is slow.
7.correctAnswer: An urban LTE resource block shows a deep notch on some subcarriers but not on others.
7.explanation: A large delay spread makes the frequency response vary and can cause inter-symbol interference.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Fast fading?
options: Channel 45 is used in a north-side cell and again in a cell four sites away.
A suburban tower planned for about a 2 kilometre radius forms one cell on the operator map.
A very long satellite symbol changes gain before it ends because the terminal is moving quickly.
At walking speed an LTE channel estimate is reused across a subframe because the fade is slow.
7.correctAnswer: A very long satellite symbol changes gain before it ends because the terminal is moving quickly.
7.explanation: The coherence time is then shorter than the symbol duration.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Slow fading?
options: A seven-cell cluster means each channel appears once in every group of seven cells.
At walking speed an LTE channel estimate is reused across a subframe because the fade is slow.
A suburban tower planned for about a 2 kilometre radius forms one cell on the operator map.
Channel 45 is used in a north-side cell and again in a cell four sites away.
7.correctAnswer: At walking speed an LTE channel estimate is reused across a subframe because the fade is slow.
7.explanation: The coherence time is then much longer than the symbol duration, so one estimate covers a burst.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Cell?
options: A suburban tower planned for about a 2 kilometre radius forms one cell on the operator map.
A call on channel 12 is degraded by another cell transmitting on channel 12 three sites away.
Channel 45 is used in a north-side cell and again in a cell four sites away.
A seven-cell cluster means each channel appears once in every group of seven cells.
7.correctAnswer: A suburban tower planned for about a 2 kilometre radius forms one cell on the operator map.
7.explanation: Users in that area are served by that site, which is the basic unit of a cellular plan.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Frequency reuse?
options: A seven-cell cluster means each channel appears once in every group of seven cells.
Channel 45 is used in a north-side cell and again in a cell four sites away.
A strong signal 200 kHz above a GSM carrier raises the floor in the wanted receiver.
A call on channel 12 is degraded by another cell transmitting on channel 12 three sites away.
7.correctAnswer: Channel 45 is used in a north-side cell and again in a cell four sites away.
7.explanation: Distance lowers co-channel interference, so a limited band can serve many cells.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Cluster size?
options: A seven-cell cluster means each channel appears once in every group of seven cells.
A voice call stays up while a car crosses from a city cell into a motorway cell.
A call on channel 12 is degraded by another cell transmitting on channel 12 three sites away.
A strong signal 200 kHz above a GSM carrier raises the floor in the wanted receiver.
7.correctAnswer: A seven-cell cluster means each channel appears once in every group of seven cells.
7.explanation: A larger cluster separates co-channel cells more, trading capacity per cell for less interference.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Co-channel interference?
options: A strong signal 200 kHz above a GSM carrier raises the floor in the wanted receiver.
A GSM phone leaves its old traffic channel and only then uses the new cell's channel.
A call on channel 12 is degraded by another cell transmitting on channel 12 three sites away.
A voice call stays up while a car crosses from a city cell into a motorway cell.
7.correctAnswer: A call on channel 12 is degraded by another cell transmitting on channel 12 three sites away.
7.explanation: Reuse places the same channel in other cells, and those signals enter the victim receiver.

7.question: Which situation illustrates Adjacent-channel interference?
options: A voice call stays up while a car crosses from a city cell into a motorway cell.
A GSM phone leaves its old traffic channel and only then uses the new cell's channel.
A UMTS phone at a cell edge exchanges traffic with two Node Bs at the same time.
A strong signal 200 kHz above a GSM carrier raises the floor in the wanted receiver.
7.correctAnswer: A strong signal 200 kHz above a GSM carrier raises the floor in the wanted receiver.
7.explanation: Imperfect filters and transmitter masks let nearby frequencies spill into the wanted channel.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Handover?
options: A voice call stays up while a car crosses from a city cell into a motorway cell.
A UMTS phone at a cell edge exchanges traffic with two Node Bs at the same time.
A GSM phone leaves its old traffic channel and only then uses the new cell's channel.
A neighbour must be at least 3 dB stronger than the serving cell before the call moves.
8.correctAnswer: A voice call stays up while a car crosses from a city cell into a motorway cell.
8.explanation: As the user moves, the radio link must follow the cell with the better signal.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Hard handover?
options: A neighbour must be at least 3 dB stronger than the serving cell before the call moves.
A GSM phone leaves its old traffic channel and only then uses the new cell's channel.
A UMTS phone at a cell edge exchanges traffic with two Node Bs at the same time.
A phone standing on a boundary is moved between two towers four times in one minute.
8.correctAnswer: A GSM phone leaves its old traffic channel and only then uses the new cell's channel.
8.explanation: The mobile cannot hold both channels at once, so there is a short break-before-make gap.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Soft handover?
options: A UMTS phone at a cell edge exchanges traffic with two Node Bs at the same time.
After a bus crosses a location-area border, the idle phone updates the network and returns to idle.
A neighbour must be at least 3 dB stronger than the serving cell before the call moves.
A phone standing on a boundary is moved between two towers four times in one minute.
8.correctAnswer: A UMTS phone at a cell edge exchanges traffic with two Node Bs at the same time.
8.explanation: CDMA can combine the same signal from several sites before one link is dropped.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Handover hysteresis?
options: A phone standing on a boundary is moved between two towers four times in one minute.
When a friend dials the number, cells in the stored area broadcast that phone's paging identity.
A neighbour must be at least 3 dB stronger than the serving cell before the call moves.
After a bus crosses a location-area border, the idle phone updates the network and returns to idle.
8.correctAnswer: A neighbour must be at least 3 dB stronger than the serving cell before the call moves.
8.explanation: The margin stops switching when two cell signals are nearly equal and fluctuating.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Ping-pong handover?
options: After a bus crosses a location-area border, the idle phone updates the network and returns to idle.
A phone standing on a boundary is moved between two towers four times in one minute.
When a friend dials the number, cells in the stored area broadcast that phone's paging identity.
A classic GSM voice call occupies one of eight slots on a 200 kHz carrier near 900 MHz.
8.correctAnswer: A phone standing on a boundary is moved between two towers four times in one minute.
8.explanation: Signal fluctuation around a tight threshold reverses the handover decision again and again.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Location update?
options: A classic GSM voice call occupies one of eight slots on a 200 kHz carrier near 900 MHz.
When a friend dials the number, cells in the stored area broadcast that phone's paging identity.
After a bus crosses a location-area border, the idle phone updates the network and returns to idle.
On a GSM carrier, one user transmits only in slot 3 of every frame.
8.correctAnswer: After a bus crosses a location-area border, the idle phone updates the network and returns to idle.
8.explanation: The network stores that area so it later knows where to page the mobile.

8.question: Which situation illustrates Paging?
options: A classic GSM voice call occupies one of eight slots on a 200 kHz carrier near 900 MHz.
When a friend dials the number, cells in the stored area broadcast that phone's paging identity.
An older trunked radio gives each active call its own 12.5 kHz channel at the same time.
On a GSM carrier, one user transmits only in slot 3 of every frame.
8.correctAnswer: When a friend dials the number, cells in the stored area broadcast that phone's paging identity.
8.explanation: The network often knows only the location area, so it calls the mobile across that area.

8.question: Which situation illustrates GSM?
options: An older trunked radio gives each active call its own 12.5 kHz channel at the same time.
On a GSM carrier, one user transmits only in slot 3 of every frame.
Two UMTS phones transmit together in the same 5 MHz block and are separated by codes.
A classic GSM voice call occupies one of eight slots on a 200 kHz carrier near 900 MHz.
8.correctAnswer: A classic GSM voice call occupies one of eight slots on a 200 kHz carrier near 900 MHz.
8.explanation: GSM carries digital voice in eight time slots on each 200 kHz GMSK carrier.

8.question: Which situation illustrates TDMA?
options: On a GSM carrier, one user transmits only in slot 3 of every frame.
An older trunked radio gives each active call its own 12.5 kHz channel at the same time.
Two UMTS phones transmit together in the same 5 MHz block and are separated by codes.
An LTE downlink gives one phone 12 subcarriers and another phone a different group in the same symbol.
8.correctAnswer: On a GSM carrier, one user transmits only in slot 3 of every frame.
8.explanation: Users transmit in turn, so they are separated in time on the same frequency.

8.question: Which situation illustrates FDMA?
options: An LTE downlink gives one phone 12 subcarriers and another phone a different group in the same symbol.
A smartphone download is scheduled as resource blocks on a 20 MHz LTE carrier.
Two UMTS phones transmit together in the same 5 MHz block and are separated by codes.
An older trunked radio gives each active call its own 12.5 kHz channel at the same time.
8.correctAnswer: An older trunked radio gives each active call its own 12.5 kHz channel at the same time.
8.explanation: Filters and guard bands keep users apart because they occupy different frequencies together.

9.question: Which situation illustrates CDMA?
options: A stadium radio uses 120 kHz subcarrier spacing and a large array near 28 GHz.
Two UMTS phones transmit together in the same 5 MHz block and are separated by codes.
An LTE downlink gives one phone 12 subcarriers and another phone a different group in the same symbol.
A smartphone download is scheduled as resource blocks on a 20 MHz LTE carrier.
9.correctAnswer: Two UMTS phones transmit together in the same 5 MHz block and are separated by codes.
9.explanation: A receiver despreads its own code and treats other users as interference.

9.question: Which situation illustrates OFDMA?
options: A smartphone download is scheduled as resource blocks on a 20 MHz LTE carrier.
A stadium radio uses 120 kHz subcarrier spacing and a large array near 28 GHz.
A cafe installs a low-power cellular radio that covers the shop and the pavement outside.
An LTE downlink gives one phone 12 subcarriers and another phone a different group in the same symbol.
9.correctAnswer: An LTE downlink gives one phone 12 subcarriers and another phone a different group in the same symbol.
9.explanation: Orthogonal subcarriers can be packed tightly and grouped to follow each user's channel.

9.question: Which situation illustrates LTE?
options: A cafe installs a low-power cellular radio that covers the shop and the pavement outside.
A Wi-Fi access point with three antennas sends two spatial streams to a two-antenna laptop.
A smartphone download is scheduled as resource blocks on a 20 MHz LTE carrier.
A stadium radio uses 120 kHz subcarrier spacing and a large array near 28 GHz.
9.correctAnswer: A smartphone download is scheduled as resource blocks on a 20 MHz LTE carrier.
9.explanation: LTE schedules packet data on a shared OFDMA carrier and does not use circuit-switched radio bearers.

9.question: Which situation illustrates 5G NR?
options: A stadium radio uses 120 kHz subcarrier spacing and a large array near 28 GHz.
A Wi-Fi access point with three antennas sends two spatial streams to a two-antenna laptop.
A cafe installs a low-power cellular radio that covers the shop and the pavement outside.
A 5G panel steers a narrow beam that follows one phone as it moves across a hall.
9.correctAnswer: A stadium radio uses 120 kHz subcarrier spacing and a large array near 28 GHz.
9.explanation: NR numerology lets one design serve wide millimetre-wave carriers and short low-latency slots.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Small cell?
options: A Wi-Fi access point with three antennas sends two spatial streams to a two-antenna laptop.
A 5G panel steers a narrow beam that follows one phone as it moves across a hall.
A campus tower with 64 antennas serves eight phones on the same resource blocks.
A cafe installs a low-power cellular radio that covers the shop and the pavement outside.
9.correctAnswer: A cafe installs a low-power cellular radio that covers the shop and the pavement outside.
9.explanation: Short range lets spectrum be reused densely and fills gaps a macro site covers poorly.

9.question: Which situation illustrates MIMO?
options: A lecture-hall laptop joins an 802.11 network advertised by the campus SSID.
A Wi-Fi access point with three antennas sends two spatial streams to a two-antenna laptop.
A campus tower with 64 antennas serves eight phones on the same resource blocks.
A 5G panel steers a narrow beam that follows one phone as it moves across a hall.
9.correctAnswer: A Wi-Fi access point with three antennas sends two spatial streams to a two-antenna laptop.
9.explanation: Scattering makes the spatial paths different enough for the receiver to separate the streams.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Beamforming?
options: A lecture-hall laptop joins an 802.11 network advertised by the campus SSID.
A campus tower with 64 antennas serves eight phones on the same resource blocks.
Two laptops both find the medium idle, then each waits a different random backoff.
A 5G panel steers a narrow beam that follows one phone as it moves across a hall.
9.correctAnswer: A 5G panel steers a narrow beam that follows one phone as it moves across a hall.
9.explanation: Phase weights make the waves add toward the user and partly cancel elsewhere.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Massive MIMO?
options: A lecture-hall laptop joins an 802.11 network advertised by the campus SSID.
A campus tower with 64 antennas serves eight phones on the same resource blocks.
Laptops on opposite sides of a pillar both transmit to one access point and corrupt each other.
Two laptops both find the medium idle, then each waits a different random backoff.
9.correctAnswer: A campus tower with 64 antennas serves eight phones on the same resource blocks.
9.explanation: Dozens or hundreds of antennas form tight beams and separate users in space.

9.question: Which situation illustrates Wi-Fi?
options: Laptops on opposite sides of a pillar both transmit to one access point and corrupt each other.
A headset stays linked to a phone across a room on a shared Bluetooth hop sequence.
Two laptops both find the medium idle, then each waits a different random backoff.
A lecture-hall laptop joins an 802.11 network advertised by the campus SSID.
9.correctAnswer: A lecture-hall laptop joins an 802.11 network advertised by the campus SSID.
9.explanation: 802.11 defines wireless LAN frames, contention access, and bands such as 2.4 and 5 GHz.

9.question: Which situation illustrates CSMA/CA?
options: A headset stays linked to a phone across a room on a shared Bluetooth hop sequence.
A radio dwells on 2402 MHz, then 2430 MHz, then 2475 MHz, following a shared pattern.
Laptops on opposite sides of a pillar both transmit to one access point and corrupt each other.
Two laptops both find the medium idle, then each waits a different random backoff.
9.correctAnswer: Two laptops both find the medium idle, then each waits a different random backoff.
9.explanation: A wireless sender cannot reliably hear a collision while it transmits, so it tries to avoid one.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Hidden node?
options: Successive symbols use the phases 45, 135, 225, and 315 degrees for bit pairs.
A radio dwells on 2402 MHz, then 2430 MHz, then 2475 MHz, following a shared pattern.
Laptops on opposite sides of a pillar both transmit to one access point and corrupt each other.
A headset stays linked to a phone across a room on a shared Bluetooth hop sequence.
10.correctAnswer: Laptops on opposite sides of a pillar both transmit to one access point and corrupt each other.
10.explanation: Distance or an obstacle hides one sender, so carrier sense does not prevent a collision.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Bluetooth?
options: A headset stays linked to a phone across a room on a shared Bluetooth hop sequence.
Successive symbols use the phases 45, 135, 225, and 315 degrees for bit pairs.
A strong Wi-Fi link uses 64-QAM so that each symbol carries six bits.
A radio dwells on 2402 MHz, then 2430 MHz, then 2475 MHz, following a shared pattern.
10.correctAnswer: A headset stays linked to a phone across a room on a shared Bluetooth hop sequence.
10.explanation: Classic Bluetooth hops among 79 one-megahertz channels to live with other 2.4 GHz users.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Frequency hopping?
options: A radio dwells on 2402 MHz, then 2430 MHz, then 2475 MHz, following a shared pattern.
A strong Wi-Fi link uses 64-QAM so that each symbol carries six bits.
Successive symbols use the phases 45, 135, 225, and 315 degrees for bit pairs.
As a user walks toward the tower, the scheduler moves the LTE MCS from QPSK toward 64-QAM.
10.correctAnswer: A radio dwells on 2402 MHz, then 2430 MHz, then 2475 MHz, following a shared pattern.
10.explanation: A narrow interferer then damages only some hops, and the link can recover the others.

10.question: Which situation illustrates QPSK?
options: A base station selects the stronger of two rooftop antennas when one sits in a deep fade.
Successive symbols use the phases 45, 135, 225, and 315 degrees for bit pairs.
As a user walks toward the tower, the scheduler moves the LTE MCS from QPSK toward 64-QAM.
A strong Wi-Fi link uses 64-QAM so that each symbol carries six bits.
10.correctAnswer: Successive symbols use the phases 45, 135, 225, and 315 degrees for bit pairs.
10.explanation: Four phases carry two bits per symbol and can keep a constant envelope.

10.question: Which situation illustrates QAM?
options: A strong Wi-Fi link uses 64-QAM so that each symbol carries six bits.
As a user walks toward the tower, the scheduler moves the LTE MCS from QPSK toward 64-QAM.
A base station selects the stronger of two rooftop antennas when one sits in a deep fade.
A tower uses three 120-degree panels, each with its own channel set.
10.correctAnswer: A strong Wi-Fi link uses 64-QAM so that each symbol carries six bits.
10.explanation: A rectangular constellation packs several bits into one symbol when the link is strong enough.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Link adaptation?
options: As a user walks toward the tower, the scheduler moves the LTE MCS from QPSK toward 64-QAM.
During a commute the core updates the tracking area and the radio network hands over the bearer.
A tower uses three 120-degree panels, each with its own channel set.
A base station selects the stronger of two rooftop antennas when one sits in a deep fade.
10.correctAnswer: As a user walks toward the tower, the scheduler moves the LTE MCS from QPSK toward 64-QAM.
10.explanation: A strong channel can use a denser constellation, while a weak channel needs a tougher mode.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Spatial diversity?
options: A base station selects the stronger of two rooftop antennas when one sits in a deep fade.
A cell-edge phone whose signal is 10 dB above interference plus noise has a SINR of 10 dB.
During a commute the core updates the tracking area and the radio network hands over the bearer.
A tower uses three 120-degree panels, each with its own channel set.
10.correctAnswer: A base station selects the stronger of two rooftop antennas when one sits in a deep fade.
10.explanation: Antennas spaced by a fraction of a wavelength see partly independent multipath.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Sectorisation?
options: A handset two kilometres from a tower receives far less power than one at 200 metres.
A cell-edge phone whose signal is 10 dB above interference plus noise has a SINR of 10 dB.
A tower uses three 120-degree panels, each with its own channel set.
During a commute the core updates the tracking area and the radio network hands over the bearer.
10.correctAnswer: A tower uses three 120-degree panels, each with its own channel set.
10.explanation: Each sector sees a smaller angle of interference and can carry its own channels.

10.question: Which situation illustrates Mobility management?
options: During a commute the core updates the tracking area and the radio network hands over the bearer.
A clear satellite downlink loses power with both distance and carrier frequency.
A cell-edge phone whose signal is 10 dB above interference plus noise has a SINR of 10 dB.
A handset two kilometres from a tower receives far less power than one at 200 metres.
10.correctAnswer: During a commute the core updates the tracking area and the radio network hands over the bearer.
10.explanation: It includes idle-area tracking and active handover so reachability and sessions survive motion.

10.question: Which situation illustrates SINR?
options: A clear satellite downlink loses power with both distance and carrier frequency.
A handset two kilometres from a tower receives far less power than one at 200 metres.
A cell-edge phone whose signal is 10 dB above interference plus noise has a SINR of 10 dB.
On a city street the same beacon reaches a phone from a wall, a bus, and the road.
10.correctAnswer: A cell-edge phone whose signal is 10 dB above interference plus noise has a SINR of 10 dB.
10.explanation: Both interference and noise corrupt symbols, so schedulers and decoders use this ratio.

11.question: Doubling the range from a tower drops received power by several decibels even on a clear path. Which effect explains that drop?
options: Paging delay
Path loss
Handover hysteresis
Ciphering overhead
11.explanation: Received power falls with distance because the wave spreads, which is path loss.

11.question: A rooftop microwave budget, with a clear line of sight, includes a loss that grows with frequency and distance. Which loss is that?
options: Free-space path loss
Coding gain
Shadowing
Adjacent-channel leakage
11.explanation: With no obstacles, distance and frequency loss is free-space path loss.

11.question: A receiver recording shows three delayed copies of one transmitted pulse. Which propagation effect produced those copies?
options: Multipath propagation
Sectorisation
Thermal noise
Power-control lag
11.explanation: Distinct delayed copies mean the signal took more than one path.

11.question: A seated laptop holds a steady Wi-Fi rate, but pacing the same room makes the rate swing. Which channel effect is the walking user seeing?
options: Fading
IP fragmentation
Clock drift
DNS caching
11.explanation: Small movements change how multipath copies combine, which is fading.

11.question: A campus model assumes no line of sight and many similar scatterers around the handset. Which envelope distribution fits?
options: Rayleigh
Constant amplitude
Uniform from zero to one
Rician
11.explanation: Many scattered paths and no dominant path give a Rayleigh envelope.

11.question: A rural link has one strong direct path plus a few ground reflections. Which fading model fits that mix?
options: Rician fading
Frequency reuse
Pure shadowing
Rayleigh fading
11.explanation: A dominant path plus weaker scatterers is the Rician case.

11.question: Over hundreds of metres the local mean wobbles as vans and buildings block a street-level user. Which large-scale effect is that?
options: A pure Doppler offset
Shadowing
Slot stealing
Fast fading
11.explanation: Obstacle blockage of the local mean is shadowing, often modelled as log-normal.

11.question: A high-speed train receiver sees the downlink carrier move by several hundred hertz. Which motion effect is that?
options: Header compression
Extra path delay
Doppler shift
Quantisation
11.explanation: Relative speed changes the received frequency, which is Doppler shift.

11.question: A designer needs how long one channel estimate remains usable for a moving user. Which quantity is that interval?
options: Beacon interval
Delay spread
Cluster size
Coherence time
11.explanation: The time the channel stays steady is the coherence time.

11.question: Engineers compare the signal bandwidth with the band where the gain stays similar. Which channel measure is that band?
options: Reuse distance
Coherence bandwidth
Hop rate
Coherence time
11.explanation: Correlation of fading across frequency is the coherence bandwidth.

12.question: Sounding shows the first echo at 0.2 microseconds and the last strong echo at 4 microseconds. Which quantity is about 3.8 microseconds?
options: Hop dwell
Delay spread
Coherence time
Timing advance
12.explanation: The span from the first to the last significant echo is the delay spread.

12.question: A 25 kHz signal has a coherence bandwidth of several hundred kilohertz. Which fading type should the link assume?
options: Flat fading
Frequency-selective fading
Adjacent-channel fading
Wideband notch fading
12.explanation: A signal narrower than the coherence bandwidth sees flat fading.

12.question: A wideband waveform sees a notch that removes only part of its spectrum. Which fading type is that?
options: Log-normal shadowing
Flat fading
Slow power-control error
Frequency-selective fading
12.explanation: A notch across only part of the band is frequency-selective fading.

12.question: The coherence time is shorter than the symbol period, so one symbol sees a changing gain. Which fading speed is that?
options: Fast fading
Static line of sight
Shadowing only
Slow fading
12.explanation: A channel that varies inside a symbol is fast fading.

12.question: Estimates taken once per subframe stay valid for dozens of symbols at pedestrian speed. Which fading speed is that?
options: Slow fading
Fast fading
Impulsive noise
Frequency-selective fading
12.explanation: A gain that holds over many symbols is slow fading.

12.question: Planners draw a hexagon around one tower to show the area that tower is meant to serve. Which planning unit is the hexagon?
options: Location area
SIM identity
Core switch
Cell
12.explanation: The area served by one base-station site is a cell.

12.question: An operator has only 60 voice channels but hundreds of cells. Which planning method lets distant cells share those channels?
options: Frequency reuse
A unique band for every cell
Cipher-key refresh
Soft combining
12.explanation: Sharing carriers among distant cells is frequency reuse.

12.question: Hexagonal planning uses shift parameters i=2 and j=1. How many cells are in one cluster?
12.explanation: Cluster size is i squared plus i times j plus j squared, which equals 7.

12.question: Two distant cells both use 935.2 MHz, and each phone hears the other cell. Which interference is that?
options: Self-echo multipath
Co-channel interference
Adjacent-channel interference
Thermal noise
12.explanation: The same carrier used in another cell produces co-channel interference.

12.question: A handset tuned to carrier f is disturbed by a nearby tower on the next 200 kHz carrier. Which interference is that?
options: Doppler spread
Code collision
Co-channel interference
Adjacent-channel interference
12.explanation: Leakage from the next carrier is adjacent-channel interference.

13.question: During a live call the serving signal falls and a neighbour becomes stronger, so the network moves the radio link. Which procedure is that?
options: Location update
Initial attach
Paging
Handover
13.explanation: Moving an active connection between cells is a handover.

13.question: A GSM call drops the old traffic channel and only afterwards uses the new cell. Which handover style is that?
options: Hard handover
Soft handover
Softer handover
Idle reselection
13.explanation: Releasing the old link before the new one is hard handover.

13.question: A CDMA phone stays in the active set of two base stations and combines both downlinks. Which handover style is that?
options: Location update
Soft handover
Hard handover
Directed retry
13.explanation: Holding links to two base stations at once is soft handover.

13.question: Two cells differ by only 1 dB and the required margin is 3 dB, so the call stays. Which parameter is blocking the move?
options: Timing advance
Speech-coding rate
Handover hysteresis
Reuse factor
13.explanation: The extra margin that must be cleared is handover hysteresis.

13.question: A stationary user on a boundary is switched between two cells every few seconds. Which handover fault is that?
options: Stable soft handover
Normal call setup
One-time cell reselection
Ping-pong handover
13.explanation: Oscillating between two cells is ping-pong handover.

13.question: An idle phone enters a new location area and must tell the network before the next incoming call. Which message does it send?
options: Location update
Handover command
Paging response
Active measurement report
13.explanation: Idle mobiles report a new location area with a location update.

13.question: An idle subscriber is called, and base stations in the stored area broadcast a request for that handset. Which procedure is the broadcast?
options: Handover
Location update
Uplink random access
Paging
13.explanation: Searching an area for an idle mobile is paging.

13.question: A legacy network puts eight users in successive slots on one 200 kHz GMSK carrier. Which cellular standard is that?
options: Bluetooth
LTE
GSM
5G NR
13.explanation: Eight-slot TDMA and GMSK on 200 kHz carriers identify GSM.

13.question: Four users share one frequency, each sending only in its own repeating slot. Which multiple-access method is that?
options: CDMA
CSMA/CA
TDMA
FDMA
13.explanation: Separation by time slots on one carrier is TDMA.

13.question: Three calls run at once on 825, 825.03, and 825.06 MHz with no time sharing. Which access method is that?
options: TDMA
FDMA
ALOHA
CDMA
13.explanation: Distinct frequencies used at the same time are FDMA.

14.question: Several users occupy the same 5 MHz block at the same time and are separated only by codes. Which access method is that?
options: TDMA
CDMA
SDMA
FDMA
14.explanation: Code separation on a shared carrier is CDMA.

14.question: A scheduler gives user A subcarriers 0-11 and user B subcarriers 24-35 in the same symbol. Which access method is that?
options: CDMA
Classic single-carrier FDMA
CSMA/CA
OFDMA
14.explanation: Assigning groups of orthogonal subcarriers is OFDMA.

14.question: A 4G air interface uses OFDMA toward the phone, SC-FDMA from the phone, and an all-IP core. Which system is that?
options: LTE
UMTS Release 99
Bluetooth
GSM
14.explanation: OFDMA downlink, SC-FDMA uplink, and an all-IP core identify LTE.

14.question: A new air interface can select 15, 30, or 120 kHz subcarrier spacing and large antenna arrays. Which standard is that?
options: LTE
Wi-Fi
GSM
5G NR
14.explanation: Scalable subcarrier spacing is a defining feature of 5G NR.

14.question: An operator adds a low-power node for one railway platform and keeps the macro tower. Which site type is the new node?
options: Macro cell
Core router
Small cell
Satellite gateway
14.explanation: A low-power, short-range base station is a small cell.

14.question: A link uses four transmit and four receive antennas to carry four independent streams on one carrier. Which technique is that?
options: Time duplexing alone
MIMO
FDMA
Receive diversity of one stream
14.explanation: Multiple independent spatial streams are MIMO.

14.question: An array applies phase shifts so the downlink adds up at one handset and is weaker elsewhere. Which technique is that?
options: Beamforming
Omnidirectional broadcast
Frequency hopping
Source coding
14.explanation: Steering array energy toward one user is beamforming.

14.question: A site uses 64 antennas to beamform many phones at once on the same subcarriers. Which architecture is that?
options: A Bluetooth piconet
Massive MIMO
A single dipole
A classic three-sector GSM site
14.explanation: A very large array serving many co-channel users is massive MIMO.

14.question: Students connect laptops to an IEEE 802.11 access point in the unlicensed 5 GHz band. Which technology is that?
options: 5G NR
GSM
Wi-Fi
LTE
14.explanation: An IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN is Wi-Fi.

14.question: A station senses the medium and, if it is idle, still waits a random number of slots before a data frame. Which method is that?
options: Pure ALOHA
CSMA/CA
CSMA/CD
TDMA
14.explanation: Listen-before-talk with random backoff is CSMA/CA.

15.question: Station A cannot hear station B, yet their frames collide at the access point between them. Which problem is that?
options: Exposed node
Capture effect
Near-far effect
Hidden node
15.explanation: Mutually hidden senders colliding at the receiver are a hidden node.

15.question: A headset and a phone keep a short-range 2.4 GHz link that hops across dozens of channels. Which technology fits?
options: Bluetooth
GSM
LTE
A geostationary satellite link
15.explanation: A short-range frequency-hopping personal link is Bluetooth.

15.question: A link changes carrier 1600 times per second using a sequence the receiver already knows. Which method is that?
options: Fixed-channel FDMA
Time hopping alone
Frequency hopping
Direct-sequence spreading
15.explanation: A shared rapid sequence of carriers is frequency hopping.

15.question: A constellation has four points on a circle, each representing a different two-bit pair. Which modulation is that?
options: 16-QAM
QPSK
OOK
BPSK
15.explanation: Four equally spaced phases and two bits per symbol identify QPSK.

15.question: A constellation is a square grid of several amplitudes and phases, with six bits on each symbol. Which family is that?
options: BPSK
OOK
QAM
BFSK
15.explanation: A grid that uses both amplitude and phase is QAM.

15.question: The scheduler selects a higher-order constellation only after the reported channel quality improves. Which technique is that?
options: Fixed modulation
Link adaptation
SIM authentication
Frequency planning
15.explanation: Matching modulation and code rate to channel quality is link adaptation.

15.question: Two receive antennas carry the same stream, and the receiver keeps the stronger branch. Which technique is that?
options: Spatial multiplexing
Source coding
Sectorisation
Spatial diversity
15.explanation: Separated antennas protecting one stream provide spatial diversity.

15.question: One site is split into three 120-degree panels, and each panel has its own channels. Which technique is that?
options: Single-channel hopping
Omnidirectional coverage
Sectorisation
Soft handover
15.explanation: Directional panels that split a site are sectorisation.

15.question: Packets must still arrive after a user changes cells and later enters a new tracking area. Which function set handles that?
options: Mobility management
Billing mediation
Speech compression
Antenna design
15.explanation: Tracking location and maintaining sessions during motion is mobility management.

15.question: A scheduler compares wanted power with interference plus noise before choosing a modulation. Which metric is it using?
options: SINR
RSSI alone
Cluster size
Delay spread
15.explanation: Wanted power over interference plus noise is SINR.
